title: Domestication, Dispersal, and Human Selection
objective: Separate evidence about domestication history from the present native-range record and modern commercial origin stories.

terms.definition: Heritable change associated with repeated human cultivation and selection.
A locally adapted, historically cultivated population; the term requires provenance and should not be used as decoration.
Movement of genetic material between populations through crossing and backcrossing.
Loss of diversity when a population is founded or propagated from few individuals.

coreScience: Cannabis has been used for fiber, food, oil-rich achenes, ritual or intoxicating preparations, and medicine. Those uses created different selection pressures. Tall, less-branched plants can be useful for stem fiber; synchronized maturity and seed production matter in grain crops; flowering architecture and glandular trichomes became important in cannabinoid-rich crops.

Genomic studies have proposed an early domestication history in East Asia and divergence among ancestral, hemp, and drug-type groups. Kew’s present taxonomic distribution record lists a native range from Central Asia to Xinjiang and Pakistan. These statements answer different questions and should not be collapsed into a single simplistic “origin.” Human dispersal and selection were major contributors to present diversity, alongside natural population history, introgression, drift, feralization, incomplete sampling, and later breeding.

Modern cannabis is not a frozen survival of ancient regional types. During the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, breeders repeatedly crossed geographic and commercial lines, selected within small populations, propagated elite clones, and renamed material. A lineage claim should therefore be treated as a documented hypothesis unless supported by preserved pedigrees, accession records, or genomic evidence.
cultivationRelevance: Domestication explains why there is no single natural growth form or universal production target. Different selection histories influence flowering, architecture, fiber allocation, seed traits, and secondary chemistry.
Genetic conservation requires population-level thinking. Preserving one clone protects one genotype; it does not preserve the diversity of a seed population.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Where the material was obtained and from whom.
Documented parents, generation, and breeder records.
Number of seeds or individuals sampled and maintained.
Traits and environments used to choose parents or keepers.
Seed lot, clones, tissue culture, or multiple backups.

misconceptions: Ancient means genetically unchanged: Cultivated populations evolve through selection, drift, crossing, and replacement.
A regional name proves landrace status: Provenance and population history are required.
One domestication paper closes the question: Conclusions depend on sampled populations, models, and archaeological interpretation.
evidenceLimits: Domestication history remains an active research area. This lesson reports the distinction between current taxonomic range and genomic hypotheses without treating either as a complete cultural history.
